warmup.q: Three worker coroutines each run for (id in ids) settle(id) over the same Channel<String>, and a producer sends 9 ids into it, then closes it. How many times is each id settled?
options: Three times: every worker gets every id
Exactly once: each element goes to one receiver
Once, but all 9 go to whichever worker started first
It can't work: only one coroutine may receive from a channel
warmup.why: A channel is a queue: each element is received by exactly one receiver. Several receivers on one channel is fan-out, and the channel serves waiting receivers fairly, so the ids spread across the three workers. Delivering every value to every subscriber is what a SharedFlow does.

sections.h: A channel is a queue between coroutines, and its capacity sets the pace
sections.html:
A Channel<T> is the coroutine version of a BlockingQueue. send puts an element in and receive takes one out, but where a blocking queue blocks a thread, a channel suspends a coroutine. Each element is received by exactly one receiver, which is the difference from a SharedFlow (lesson 8 of this track), where every subscriber gets every value.

Java
// Java equivalent: a bounded BlockingQueue, with an end marker because a queue can't be closed
BlockingQueue<String> ids = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(64);
Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> {
    for (String id : batchIds) putQuietly(ids, id);   // blocks while the queue is full
    putQuietly(ids, END);
});
for (String id = ids.take(); !id.equals(END); id = ids.take()) settle(id);
Kotlin
val ids = Channel<String>(capacity = 64)
launch {
    for (id in batchIds) ids.send(id)   // suspends while the buffer is full
    ids.close()                         // no more elements: the receiving loop will end
}
for (id in ids) settle(id)              // receives until the channel is closed and empty

The capacity decides how far a sender can run ahead of the receiver:

Capacity send suspends when Like
Channel.RENDEZVOUS (0, the default) no receiver is waiting SynchronousQueue
Channel(n) n elements are already waiting ArrayBlockingQueue(n)
Channel.BUFFERED 64 are waiting (a JVM property changes the default) ArrayBlockingQueue(64)
Channel.UNLIMITED never: memory is the limit LinkedBlockingQueue
Channel.CONFLATED never: a new element replaces the waiting one no JDK equivalent

Rendezvous is the default for a good reason: it gives you backpressure for free, because a fast producer simply waits for the consumer. Add a buffer to absorb bursts. Be suspicious of UNLIMITED, which turns a slow consumer into an OutOfMemoryError some hours later.

Close a channel when you are done sending. for (x in channel) ends only when the channel is closed and empty, so a receiver on a channel nobody closes waits forever. The produce { } builder takes care of it. It starts a coroutine that sends into a new channel, closes the channel when the block ends or fails, and returns it as a ReceiveChannel. It is still marked @ExperimentalCoroutinesApi, so it needs an opt-in.

A channel is hot. Elements sit in it whether or not anyone receives, and a coroutine suspended in send never finishes until someone does. For a stream with a single consumer, a cold Flow is usually the better tool. Channels are for coroutines that hand work to each other.

code.title: ChannelCapacities.kt
code.html: package workbench.coroutines.l09 import kotlinx.coroutines.channels.Channel import kotlinx.coroutines.coroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking /** A producer sends 5 batch ids as fast as it can; the consumer needs 100 ms per id. */ suspend fun run(label: String, channel: Channel<Int>) = coroutineScope { val t0 = System.nanoTime() fun ms() = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 val sendTimes = mutableListOf<Long>() launch { for (id in 1..5) { channel.send(id); sendTimes += ms() } channel.close() // no more ids: the consumer's for loop ends after the last one } val received = mutableListOf<Int>() for (id in channel) { delay(100); received += id } println("%-12s send() returned at %-26s received %s".format(label, sendTimes.toString() + " ms", received)) } fun main() = runBlocking { run("RENDEZVOUS", Channel(Channel.RENDEZVOUS)) run("capacity 2", Channel(2)) run("UNLIMITED", Channel(Channel.UNLIMITED)) run("CONFLATED", Channel(Channel.CONFLATED)) }

alt.title: ChannelCapacitiesJava.java
alt.html: // Java equivalent of ChannelCapacities.kt: blocking queues between two threads. SynchronousQueue // is a rendezvous, ArrayBlockingQueue(2) has capacity 2, LinkedBlockingQueue is unbounded. // The JDK has no conflated queue; Kotlin's CONFLATED channel keeps only the newest element. // A blocking queue has no close(), so the producer sends a marker (-1) at the end instead. package workbench.coroutines.l09; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue; import java.util.concurrent.BlockingQueue; import java.util.concurrent.LinkedBlockingQueue; import java.util.concurrent.SynchronousQueue; public class ChannelCapacitiesJava { static void run(String label, BlockingQueue<Integer> queue) throws InterruptedException { long t0 = System.nanoTime(); List<Long> sendTimes = new ArrayList<>(); Thread producer = Thread.ofPlatform().start(() -> { try { for (int id = 1; id <= 5; id++) { queue.put(id); sendTimes.add((System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000); } queue.put(-1); // the end marker } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }); List<Integer> received = new ArrayList<>(); for (int id = queue.take(); id != -1; id = queue.take()) { Thread.sleep(100); received.add(id); } producer.join(); System.out.printf("%-22s put() returned at %-26s received %s%n", label, sendTimes + " ms", received); } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { run("SynchronousQueue", new SynchronousQueue<>()); run("ArrayBlockingQueue(2)", new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(2)); run("LinkedBlockingQueue", new LinkedBlockingQueue<>()); } }

try.expect: Rendezvous: each send returns about 100 ms after the previous one, in step with the consumer. Capacity 2: the first three return at once (two buffered, one handed straight to the waiting receiver), then one every 100 ms. Unlimited: all five at once. Conflated: all five at once, but only [1, 5] is received, because each new id replaced the waiting one. Without close() the program never ends: the for loop waits for an id that will never come (stop it with Ctrl+C). The Java twin's three queues match the first three rows.

sections.h: Fan out to a fixed set of workers, fan in to one channel
sections.html:
Fan-out means several coroutines receive from the same channel. Each element goes to exactly one of them, and channels are fair: receivers waiting in line are served in the order they asked. So one channel plus N worker coroutines is a worker pool with a concurrency limit of N, and no thread pool is involved.

Java
// Java equivalent: a fixed pool takes tasks from its queue, a CompletionService collects results
Map<String, String> settleAll(List<String> ids, int workers) throws Exception {
    try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(workers)) {
        CompletionService<Map.Entry<String, String>> receipts = new ExecutorCompletionService<>(pool);
        for (String id : ids) receipts.submit(() -> Map.entry(id, settle(id)));
        Map<String, String> result = new HashMap<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < ids.size(); i++) { var e = receipts.take().get(); result.put(e.getKey(), e.getValue()); }
        return result;
    }
}
Kotlin
suspend fun settleAll(ids: List<String>, workers: Int): Map<String, String> = coroutineScope {
    val queue = produce { ids.forEach { send(it) } }                // fan-out source
    val receipts = Channel<Pair<String, String>>()                 // fan-in
    val pool = List(workers) { launch { for (id in queue) receipts.send(id to settle(id)) } }
    launch { pool.joinAll(); receipts.close() }                    // close once every worker is done
    val result = mutableMapOf<String, String>()
    for ((id, receipt) in receipts) result[id] = receipt
    result
}

Fan-in is the reverse: many senders, one channel, one receiver. The hard part is knowing when to close the fan-in channel. Close it too early and a worker's send throws ClosedSendChannelException. Never close it and the receiving loop waits forever. A separate coroutine that does joinAll() and then close() is the usual answer.

Everything sits inside coroutineScope, so the pipeline is structured (lesson 3 of this track). If one settle throws, the scope cancels the producer, the other workers and the closer, and rethrows. No coroutine is left waiting on a channel.

Why not ids.map { async { settle(it) } }.awaitAll()? Because that starts all 10,000 calls at once, and the acquirer will not thank you. The worker pool caps them at N. A Semaphore would cap them too (lesson 10 of this track), but a pool of workers also gives each worker a natural home for its own state, such as one connection per worker. And it composes into multi-stage pipelines, with a channel between each stage: parse, then enrich, then post, each stage with as many workers as it needs.

code.title: FanOutFanIn.kt
code.html: package workbench.coroutines.l09 import kotlinx.coroutines.ExperimentalCoroutinesApi import kotlinx.coroutines.channels.Channel import kotlinx.coroutines.channels.produce import kotlinx.coroutines.coroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.joinAll import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlin.random.Random @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class) fun main(args: Array<String>) = runBlocking { val workers = args.firstOrNull()?.toInt() ?: 4 val t0 = System.nanoTime() coroutineScope { // 1. one producer: 20 refund ids, sent one at a time val refunds = produce { for (i in 1..20) send("refund-$i") } // 2. fan-out: each id goes to exactly one worker val results = Channel<String>() val pool = List(workers) { w -> launch { for (id in refunds) { delay(Random.nextLong(50, 150)) // the issuer call results.send("$id by worker $w") } } } // 3. fan-in: close results when every worker is done launch { pool.joinAll(); results.close() } val perWorker = mutableMapOf<String, Int>() for (r in results) perWorker.merge(r.substringAfter("by "), 1, Int::plus) println("$workers workers: ${perWorker.toSortedMap()}") } println("20 refunds took ${(System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000} ms") }

sections.h: Use select to wait for whichever happens first
sections.html:
select { } suspends until the first of several clauses can complete, runs that clause, and drops the rest. The clauses are things you can wait on: deferred.onAwait, channel.onReceive, channel.onSend(value) and onTimeout(ms).

The classic payments use is hedging: ask two acquirers for a quote and take whichever answers first.

Java
// Java equivalent: anyOf completes with the first future, completeOnTimeout adds a fallback
Object first = CompletableFuture.anyOf(north, east)
    .completeOnTimeout(defaultQuote, 500, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)
    .join();
north.cancel(true); east.cancel(true);       // marks the futures; the HTTP calls may run on
Quote quote = (Quote) first;
Kotlin
val quote = coroutineScope {
    val north = async { northAcquirer.quote(req) }
    val east = async { eastAcquirer.quote(req) }
    val first = select {
        north.onAwait { it }
        east.onAwait { it }
        onTimeout(500) { defaultQuote }      // needs @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class)
    }
    north.cancel(); east.cancel()            // stop the losers
    first
}

Three details matter. select is biased: if several clauses are ready at the same moment, the first one listed wins, so list the source you prefer first. Stopping the losers is your job, just as with anyOf, but with coroutines the cancel actually reaches the losing calls at their next suspension point instead of only marking a future as cancelled. And the API status is mixed: in 1.11 the select builder compiles without an opt-in, while the guide still calls select expressions experimental and onTimeout needs @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class).

Without the timeout clause, this is also what the lab's fastestQuote does, generalized to a list: select { calls.forEach { c -> c.onAwait { it } } }.

select over the onReceive clauses of several channels can merge streams by hand. For most merging, Flow operators such as merge and combine are simpler and harder to get wrong. Keep select for "the first of these, then stop", and for the rare loop that must react to whichever of several channels has something.

sections.h: Channels inside flows: callbackFlow, channelFlow and the backpressure operators
sections.html:
A flow is sequential, so emit may only be called from the flow's own coroutine (lesson 7 of this track). When values come from somewhere else, such as a listener API or several coroutines at once, callbackFlow and channelFlow put a channel inside the flow. Producers send or trySend into it, and the collector receives from it.

callbackFlow is the bridge for listener APIs that call you many times:

Java
// Java equivalent: Flux.create with a sink, and onDispose for the cleanup
Flux<PaymentEvent> events(PaymentEventBus bus) {
    return Flux.create(sink -> {
        Registration registration = bus.register(sink::next);
        sink.onDispose(registration::unregister);
    });
}
Kotlin
fun PaymentEventBus.events(): Flow<PaymentEvent> = callbackFlow {
    val registration = register { event -> trySend(event) }   // called on the bus's thread
    awaitClose { registration.unregister() }                   // runs when the collector stops
}

awaitClose is not optional. It suspends until the collector goes away, then runs the cleanup. Without it the block returns right after registering, and callbackFlow throws IllegalStateException to stop you leaking the listener. From the callback, use trySend: it never blocks the caller's thread, and it fails if the buffer (64 by default) is full. For a callback that fires once, suspendCancellableCoroutine from lesson 1 of this track is the right tool. channelFlow is the same idea for your own coroutines: launch several producers inside it, and each one can send safely.

The other place channels hide is the backpressure operators. Take the guide's numbers: a producer that needs 100 ms per item, a collector that needs 300 ms, three items.

Pipeline The collector sees Time
plain 1, 2, 3 about 1,200 ms: (100 + 300) x 3
buffer() 1, 2, 3 about 1,000 ms: the producer runs ahead
conflate() 1, 3 about 700 ms: a busy collector skips to the latest
collectLatest { } starts 1, 2 and 3, finishes only 3 about 600 ms: a new value cancels the old work

buffer keeps everything and lets the producer run ahead into a channel. conflate keeps only the latest value, which suits prices and never suits payments. collectLatest cancels and restarts the collector's block for each new value, which suits "recompute the quote whenever the input changes". It is wrong for anything with side effects you can't take back, because the cancelled run may have done half its work.

All three trade memory, completeness and freshness against each other, and the plain flow is the safe default. Reactor's onBackpressureBuffer, onBackpressureLatest and switchMap (lesson 7 of the reactive track) make the same three trades.

code.title: FlowBackpressure.kt
code.html: package workbench.coroutines.l09 import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.Flow import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.buffer import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.collectLatest import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.conflate import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.flow import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlin.system.measureTimeMillis /** Three FX ticks, 100 ms apart. */ fun ticks(): Flow<Int> = flow { for (i in 1..3) { delay(100); emit(i) } } fun main() = runBlocking { // the collector takes 300 ms per tick (pricing a quote book) val plain = measureTimeMillis { ticks().collect { delay(300); print("$it ") } } println(" plain: $plain ms") val buffered = measureTimeMillis { ticks().buffer().collect { delay(300); print("$it ") } } println(" buffer(): $buffered ms") val conflated = measureTimeMillis { ticks().conflate().collect { delay(300); print("$it ") } } println(" conflate(): $conflated ms") val latest = measureTimeMillis { ticks().collectLatest { print("start $it, "); delay(300); print("done $it ") } } println(" collectLatest: $latest ms") }

alt.title: FlowBackpressureJava.java
alt.html: // Java equivalent of FlowBackpressure.kt with Reactor: concatMap with prefetch 0 (ask for the // next tick only when the last one is priced) is close to a plain flow, onBackpressureBuffer to buffer(), onBackpressureLatest to conflate(), and switchMap // to collectLatest (a new tick cancels the work on the previous one). package workbench.coroutines.l09; import java.time.Duration; import java.util.function.Function; import reactor.core.publisher.Flux; import reactor.core.publisher.Mono; public class FlowBackpressureJava { /** Three FX ticks, 100 ms apart, produced only when asked for (like a cold flow). */ static Flux<Integer> ticks() { return Flux.range(1, 3).concatMap(i -> Mono.just(i).delayElement(Duration.ofMillis(100)), 1); } /** Pricing a quote book: 300 ms per tick. */ static Mono<Integer> price(int i) { return Mono.just(i).delayElement(Duration.ofMillis(300)).doOnNext(x -> System.out.print(x + " ")); } static void time(String label, Function<Flux<Integer>, Flux<Integer>> pipeline) { long t0 = System.nanoTime(); pipeline.apply(ticks()).blockLast(); System.out.printf(" %-26s %d ms%n", label, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000); } public static void main(String[] args) { time("concatMap, prefetch 0:", f -> f.concatMap(FlowBackpressureJava::price, 0)); time("onBackpressureBuffer:", f -> f.onBackpressureBuffer().concatMap(FlowBackpressureJava::price, 0)); time("onBackpressureLatest:", f -> f.onBackpressureLatest().concatMap(FlowBackpressureJava::price, 0)); time("switchMap:", f -> f.switchMap(FlowBackpressureJava::price)); } }

try.expect: Plain: 1 2 3 in about 1,200 ms. buffer(): 1 2 3 in about 1,000 ms. conflate(): 1 3 in about 700 ms. collectLatest: start 1, start 2, start 3, done 3 in about 600 ms. With a 50 ms collector, conflate() prints 1 2 3: it only skips values that arrive while the collector is busy, and now it never is. The Java twin prints the same values in about the same times with concatMap, onBackpressureBuffer, onBackpressureLatest and switchMap.

analogy: A channel is the hatch between a restaurant's kitchen and its dining room. With a rendezvous hatch there is no shelf: the cook holds the plate until a waiter takes it. A buffered hatch has a shelf with a fixed number of spots, and the cook waits only when the shelf is full. Fan-out is several waiters taking plates from the same hatch, each plate going to exactly one of them. Fan-in is several cooks passing plates through one hatch to one waiter. select is ringing two suppliers and going with whoever picks up first, then hanging up on the other. The analogy breaks at closing time: in a real kitchen the staff see the lights go off. A channel's receivers only learn that nothing more is coming when someone calls close(), and if nobody does, they wait at the hatch forever.
world: A worker pool over a channel is a good fit for settlement and refund batches: size the pool to what the acquirer allows (say, 8 concurrent calls), and the channel keeps everything else waiting without holding a thread. Rendezvous or small buffers keep memory flat when the acquirer slows down. select with onAwait and onTimeout is the shape of a hedged authorization or a fallback acquirer: take the first answer within 800 ms, otherwise route elsewhere, and cancel what you no longer need. callbackFlow is how a legacy listener API, such as a fraud engine's event callbacks or a JMS listener, becomes a Flow with clean unregistering. For a Kafka consumer, keep offset commits in order: a fan-out pool processes records out of order, so commit only what every worker has finished, or keep one worker per partition.
mistake: The most common mistake is a channel that nobody closes, or a callbackFlow without awaitClose. In the first case the receiving for loop never ends, so the coroutineScope around it never returns, and the request hangs with no error and no CPU use. In the second, callbackFlow throws IllegalStateException the first time it is collected, and the fix people reach for, an awaitCancellation() or a delay(Long.MAX_VALUE), keeps the flow open but never unregisters the listener. Use produce { }, which closes its channel when the block ends; close fan-in channels after joinAll(); and end every callbackFlow with awaitClose { unregister() }.

compare.title: A capped worker pool: ExecutorService vs channel and coroutines

java.title: RefundRunner.java
java.html: List<String> refundAll(List<String> ids) throws Exception { try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8)) { // 1. 8 threads = at most 8 calls CompletionService<String> done = new ExecutorCompletionService<>(pool); for (String id : ids) done.submit(() -> issuer.refund(id)); // 2. every task queued up front List<String> receipts = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < ids.size(); i++) receipts.add(done.take().get()); // 3. fan-in, in finish order return receipts; } // a failure surfaces at get(); the other tasks keep running until close() waits for them }

kotlin.title: RefundRunner.kt
kotlin.html: suspend fun refundAll(ids: List<String>): List<String> = coroutineScope { val queue = produce { ids.forEach { send(it) } } // 2. ids handed out one at a time val receipts = Channel<String>() val pool = List(8) { launch { for (id in queue) receipts.send(issuer.refund(id)) } } // 1. 8 workers launch { pool.joinAll(); receipts.close() } val result = mutableListOf<String>() for (r in receipts) result += r // 3. fan-in, in finish order result } // a failure cancels the producer and every worker, then rethrows

compare.note: Both cap the issuer at 8 concurrent refunds and collect results in the order they finish. The Java version spends 8 threads, which sit blocked while the issuer thinks, and it queues every task up front. The Kotlin version spends 8 coroutines, which suspend while waiting, and the rendezvous channel hands out ids only as workers free up, so a list of a million ids never sits in a task queue. The bigger difference is failure. In Java one failed refund shows up at get(), and the other tasks keep running until close() waits for them. In Kotlin the whole pipeline is one coroutineScope, so the first failure cancels the producer and every worker before the exception reaches the caller.

steps.say: An acquirer's settlement file has 200,000 lines. Each line must be parsed, enriched with a BIN lookup (a blocking legacy client, 20 ms per call), and posted to the ledger in batches of 500. Doing it in one loop takes over an hour, almost all of it in BIN lookups.
steps.code: suspend fun importFile(reader: LineReader) { val batch = mutableListOf<Posting>() while (true) { val line = reader.readLine() ?: break val rec = parse(line) val bin = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { binClient.lookup(rec.cardBin) } // 20 ms, one at a time batch += Posting(rec, bin) if (batch.size == 500) { ledger.post(batch.toList()); batch.clear() } } if (batch.isNotEmpty()) ledger.post(batch) }

alt.html: // Java equivalent of the same single loop void importFile(LineReader reader) { List<Posting> batch = new ArrayList<>(); for (String line = reader.readLine(); line != null; line = reader.readLine()) { Record rec = parse(line); BinInfo bin = binClient.lookup(rec.cardBin()); // 20 ms, one at a time batch.add(new Posting(rec, bin)); if (batch.size() == 500) { ledger.post(List.copyOf(batch)); batch.clear(); } } if (!batch.isEmpty()) ledger.post(batch); }

steps.say: Stage 1 reads and parses on IO, into a small buffer. produce closes the channel when the file ends.
steps.code: @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class) suspend fun importFile(reader: LineReader) = coroutineScope { // 1. parse: one reader, a little ahead of the enrichers val records = produce(Dispatchers.IO, capacity = 100) { while (true) send(parse(reader.readLine() ?: break)) }

alt.html: void importFile(LineReader reader) throws Exception { // 1. parse: one reader thread, a little ahead of the enrichers BlockingQueue<Record> records = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(100); Thread parser = Thread.ofPlatform().start(() -> { for (String line = reader.readLine(); line != null; line = reader.readLine()) putQuietly(records, parse(line)); putQuietly(records, Record.END); });

steps.say: Stage 2 fans out to 16 enrichers, the BIN service's limit. They fan in to one channel, closed when all 16 are done.
steps.code: // 2. enrich: 16 workers on IO, because the BIN client blocks val postings = Channel<Posting>(capacity = 1_000) val enrichers = List(16) { launch(Dispatchers.IO) { for (rec in records) postings.send(Posting(rec, binClient.lookup(rec.cardBin))) } } launch { enrichers.joinAll(); postings.close() }

alt.html: // 2. enrich: 16 threads, because the BIN client blocks BlockingQueue<Posting> postings = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(1_000); ExecutorService enrichers = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(16); for (int i = 0; i < 16; i++) enrichers.submit(() -> { for (Record rec = records.take(); rec != Record.END; rec = records.take()) postings.put(new Posting(rec, binClient.lookup(rec.cardBin()))); records.put(Record.END); // pass the end marker on to the next enricher return null; });

steps.say: Stage 3 is a single writer, so ledger batches stay simple. When postings is closed and drained, the loop ends, and coroutineScope returns once every stage has finished. If any stage throws, the scope cancels the others.
steps.code: // 3. post: one writer, batches of 500 val batch = mutableListOf<Posting>() for (p in postings) { batch += p if (batch.size == 500) { ledger.post(batch.toList()); batch.clear() } } if (batch.isNotEmpty()) ledger.post(batch) }

alt.html: // 3. post: one writer, batches of 500 (the end of stage 2 needs its own marker or a latch) enrichers.shutdown(); List<Posting> batch = new ArrayList<>(); while (!(enrichers.isTerminated() && postings.isEmpty())) { Posting p = postings.poll(100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); if (p == null) continue; batch.add(p); if (batch.size() == 500) { ledger.post(List.copyOf(batch)); batch.clear(); } } if (!batch.isEmpty()) ledger.post(batch); parser.join(); }

steps.say: Self-check: the ledger slows to a crawl. Trace what happens to memory and to the BIN service. (The writer falls behind, postings fills up to 1,000, the enrichers suspend in send, records fills up to 100, and the parser suspends too. Memory stays flat, and the BIN service sees fewer calls. Backpressure flows all the way back to the file read.)

lab.title: A worker pool, an event bridge and a hedged quote
steps: Run the tests. Five of seven fail. PipelineModel.kt has the bus, its Registration and Quote.

In ParallelSettlement.kt, build the pool inside coroutineScope: produce the ids, start workers coroutines that loop over the ids channel and send id to settle(id) into a receipts channel, close receipts after joinAll(), and read it into a map.
In EventBusFlow.kt, keep the Registration that register returns, and end the block with awaitClose { registration.unregister() }.
In FastestQuote.kt, start every call with async, select on their onAwait clauses, cancel all the calls, and return the winner.
Run the tests until all seven pass.
hints: produce needs @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class) on the function. It closes its channel when its block ends.
Close the receipts channel from its own coroutine: launch { pool.joinAll(); receipts.close() }. If you close it after the receiving loop, the loop never ends.
awaitClose comes from kotlinx.coroutines.channels. It suspends until the collector stops, so it must be the last line of the callbackFlow block.
select { calls.forEach { c -> c.onAwait { it } } } is a whole select: the lambda registers one clause per call. Cancelling a call that already finished does nothing, so you can cancel them all.

drill.title: A capped worker pool from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write suspend fun refundAll(ids: List<String>) that calls the suspend function refund(id) for every id, with at most 3 calls running at once, using a channel and 3 worker coroutines. It returns when every refund is done, and a failure in any refund cancels the rest.

answer.html: @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class) suspend fun refundAll(ids: List<String>) = coroutineScope { val queue = produce { for (id in ids) send(id) } // closed when the block ends repeat(3) { launch { for (id in queue) refund(id) } // each id goes to one worker } } // coroutineScope waits for the producer and all three workers

alt.title: Java equivalent
alt.html: // Java equivalent: a pool of 3 threads, and invokeAll to wait for every task void refundAll(List<String> ids) throws Exception { try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(3)) { List<Callable<Void>> tasks = ids.stream() .<Callable<Void>>map(id -> () -> { refund(id); return null; }) .toList(); for (Future<Void> f : pool.invokeAll(tasks)) f.get(); // rethrows the first failure } // unlike coroutineScope, the other refunds are not cancelled on a failure }

recap: A Channel hands each element to exactly one receiver. send and receive suspend instead of blocking.
Capacity sets the pace: rendezvous (the default) hands over directly, Channel(n) buffers n, UNLIMITED never suspends (and can run out of memory), CONFLATED keeps only the newest.
Close a channel when sending is done, or for (x in channel) never ends. produce { } closes its channel for you.
Fan-out (several workers on one channel) caps concurrency at the number of workers. Fan-in channels close after joinAll(). Inside coroutineScope, one failure cancels the whole pipeline.
select takes whichever clause completes first (onAwait, onReceive, onTimeout). It is biased to the first clause, and stopping the losers is your job.
callbackFlow bridges listener APIs and must end with awaitClose { unregister() }. buffer, conflate and collectLatest trade completeness for speed or freshness.

explain.prompt: A teammate wants to settle 50,000 batches with batchIds.map { async { settle(it) } }.awaitAll(), and the acquirer allows 8 concurrent calls. Explain the problem and how a channel-based worker pool fixes it.
explain.answer: That code starts 50,000 coroutines at once, so the acquirer sees 50,000 concurrent calls, far more than its limit of 8. We'd get rate-limited or time out, and we'd hold 50,000 pending requests in memory. With a channel, one producer sends the ids into a rendezvous channel and 8 worker coroutines loop over it. Each id goes to exactly one worker, so at most 8 settle calls are in flight, and the producer just waits until a worker is free, which keeps memory flat. The workers send their receipts into a second channel that one loop reads, and a separate coroutine closes it after all the workers finish so that loop can end. Because it all runs inside coroutineScope, one failed settle cancels the producer and the other workers and the exception reaches the caller.

deeper.html:
actor { }, which older tutorials use to protect shared state with a channel of messages, is marked @ObsoleteCoroutinesApi: the KDoc says it will become obsolete when "complex actors" arrive. A plain coroutine looping over a channel you create does the same job without the warning. BroadcastChannel was deprecated in 1.7, and its deprecation level was raised in 1.9. Use SharedFlow (lesson 8 of this track) for one-to-many.

The BUFFERED default of 64 comes from the JVM system property kotlinx.coroutines.channels.defaultBuffer. It is also the buffer flowOn, buffer(), channelFlow and callbackFlow use unless you pass a size. When you size a pipeline for memory, count those hidden buffers too.

Channels also have trySend and tryReceive, which never suspend and return a ChannelResult. They are for code at the edge that can't suspend, like a listener callback, and trySendBlocking is the blocking variant for a plain thread that may wait. Since kotlinx.coroutines 1.11, ReceiveChannel.consumeTo(collection) drains a channel into a collection.

The prime-sieve pipeline in the official channels guide is a fun read: each prime gets its own filtering coroutine, chained by channels, so the pipeline grows as it runs. It is a good picture of how cheap coroutines and channels are, and a poor model for production code, where a fixed number of stages with a known number of workers is far easier to monitor and to cancel.
